newsitem.title: INDIA: India hunts for clues to worst mid-air disaster.
newsitem.headline: India hunts for clues to worst mid-air disaster.

text.p: Searchers recovered the so-called "black boxes" which should reveal what caused the world's worst mid-air collision near New Delhi that killed some 350 people, officials said on Wednesday.
The flight data and cockpit voice recorders were picked out of the horrendous debris littering the two crash sites on the north Indian plain, 80 km (50 miles) west of New Delhi.

There were no survivors among the 312 people aboard a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 that had just taken off from New Delhi on Tuesday evening or among the 37 people on a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter that was preparing to land.
Local residents said they were sure the pilot of the jumbo averted an even worse disaster by steering his blazing aircraft away from their villages.
Parveen Kumar of Charkhi Dadri town, which has a population of 50,000, told Reuters: "The plane turned into a fireball and separated into three fireballs and fell into Dadri.
"I think the pilot deliberately went over the town and tried to land in fields."
Speculation on the cause of the collision ranged from inadequate equipment at New Delhi airport to pilot misunderstanding of instructions from ground controllers.

Yogesh Chandra, the top civil servant at India's Civil Aviation Ministry, ruled out both. He said the transcript of the final conversations between the pilots and ground control showed both understood their instructions.
Speculation that aging equipment at Delhi airport might be to blame was "absolutely incorrect", he told a news conference.

Chandra refused comment on other possible causes raised by experts, including speculation the pilot of the KazAir plane could have misconverted the altitude instructions he was given in feet, the international norm.

Aircraft in the former Soviet Union use metres and unless they have altimeters showing altitude in both feet and metres, pilots use a table for conversion. But aviation experts said all Il-76 aircraft were equipped with gauges showing distances in feet in addition to the metric system.
"What the pilots did after this exchange of conversation is something that can only come out once the black boxes are decoded," Chandra said.

The recorders in the Ilyushin-76TD cargo freighter would have to be taken to Moscow to be decoded by experts there, Chandra said. Indian authorities could decode the Boeing's flight data and cockpit voice recorders.
Aviation experts said it could take less than two weeks to decode the contents of the recorders.

"I would imagine that you would begin to have some information in less than two weeks," Stuart Matthews, chairman of the U.S.-based Flight Safety Foundation, told Reuters on the sidelines of an international aviation safety meeting in Dubai.

Officials said other control tower recordings had been sealed and would be given to High Court judge R.C. Lahoti, who was appointed to conduct an inquiry. An official announcement did not say when it would begin.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda visited the crash sites after searchers toiled through darkness to pick charred and mangled bodies from the debris after the two aircraft plunged to earth in flames 10 km (six miles) apart on a clear night.
He told reporters if an individual was to blame "we will not spare any culprit" and the government would implement whatever recommendations Lahoti made after his inquiry.

A Saudi newspaper said the victims included 215 Indians, 13 Saudis, nine Nepalis and three Pakistanis. But Nepal's Foreign Ministry said there were 53 Nepalis on board. Most of them were headed for jobs as manual labourers, drivers and plumbers.
Two unidentified American women were aboard, as well as a British woman returning to her job in Saudi Arabia from a holiday in India.
The wreckage of the Saudi plane was still smoking at dusk as searchers probed it for up to 60 more bodies they estimated still remained under the debris.
Aboard the KazAir plane were 25 businessmen who had chartered the aircraft to fly empty to Delhi.

They were carrying $1.5 million in cash and had intended to fill it with Indian woollens for sale at home, KazAir Delhi airport manager Rajiv Bhaskar said. India's Chandra said police found $37,000 in the wreckage of the Kazakh aircraft.
Bhaskar said there were also two children and 10 crew on the plane, which broke in two. All 37 bodies were recovered.
Only the tail section of the Saudi aircraft, carrying mostly Indian workers, was reasonably intact after it smashed into the ground and left a 20-foot (six-metre) crater.
Seats stood upright, dinner trolleys and unbroken crockery sat forlorn in the fields as rescue workers tramped past suitcases, letters and photographs scattered in the dirt.
Some suitcases were empty and local people said there had been looting. "There should be at least one person wearing a watch but we don't find any," local businessman Vinod Garg said.
